The @dailychartbook nightly email had a chart from Fidelity’s @TimmerFidelity, which no surprise was wonderful, showing the peak of five-year S&P 500 EPS growth for every earnings cycle since the 1920s. As he notes, outside the Great Depression, growth has always topped out around the 14%–15% annualized pace we hit this cycle (around January on his chart). What stands out to him is that Bloomberg estimates call for “a modest slowdown to 12% and then a re-acceleration back to 14%.”

That path has never happened. Running the same cycles through Robert Shiller’s long-run S&P 500 data:

▪️ The median slowdown in 5-year EPS growth in the two years after a peak was about 8 points. The shallowest was 3.5 points (1976–78). The Street is looking for about 3.
▪️ In 9 of 13 cycles, growth was still falling two years out.
▪️ Only one cycle got back to its peak pace within three years (2018–21), and that was the Covid crash and rebound.

The good news is that the peak itself has been a relatively modest headwind to stocks:
▪️ Three months after the 14 peaks, the S&P 500 averaged +0.8% (versus +2.0% for any three months since 1926) and was up just half the time.
▪️ At six months it was +2.8% versus +4.1%.
▪️ By 12 months the gap was gone: +8.8% versus +8.5%, and positive 71% of the time versus 70%.
▪️ This cycle has already far exceeded historic performance, with the S&P up about 8% six months after the January peak.

So what does that mean for stocks? Every earlier cycle went through a much deeper slowdown than the Street is penciling in now, and stocks still caught up within a year. If the estimates hold, that beats the usual script. If they get cut back toward the historical path, that’s roughly what the market has always had to work through.

@C_Barraud's Friday Brief had an article from ZeroHedge on the record October budget deficit, which suffered from both increased expenses and decreased revenues. 

The deficit came in at $404B, a record for October and up $120B (42%) from a year ago. Treasury notes though after adjusting for November payments that shifted into October in both years it is a smaller $285B, but that’s still up 49% from last year.

On the expense side, outlays rose $84B (12%) to a record October $773B:

▪️ Defense rose $29B to $129B. Part of that was a military trust fund payment delayed by last year’s government shutdown; the rest came from operations, maintenance and procurement.
▪️ Medicare rose $19B to $170B.
▪️ Agriculture more than tripled to $18B on farm relief payments.
▪️ Net interest rose $12B to $103B. Over the past 12 months it totals $1.06T, more than defense and close to Medicare.
▪️ Social Security rose $9B to $143B.

On the revenue side, receipts fell $35B (9%) to $369B:
▪️ Individual income taxes not withheld from paychecks fell $29B. Last October was boosted by payments from Californians whose filing deadlines were pushed back after the wildfires.
▪️ Net customs duties fell to $19B from $31B. Refunds of the tariffs struck down by the Supreme Court were $7B, up from $2B a year ago, and gross collections slowed.
▪️ Income taxes withheld from paychecks were flat at $156B even as payroll taxes rose 4%, which is consistent with the new tax law lowering withholding.

And unfortunately it will likely get worse before it gets better (on a year-over-year basis). Spending is still growing about 5% a year, while tariff revenue is running about $10B a month below last winter’s peak while paycheck withholding is flat under the new tax law.

Many have argued that Jensen Huang’s troubles are Nvidia’s rivals’ gain. This week’s price action roughly bears that out, at least until today.

Cumulative change in market value since the November 6 close, Nvidia vs. AMD + Broadcom + Marvell combined:

▪️ Monday: Nvidia −$192B, rivals +$233B (1.21x).
▪️ Tuesday: −$428B vs. +$303B (0.71x), as Nvidia’s 5.5% drop outran its rivals' gains.
▪️ Wednesday: −$311B vs. +$441B (1.42x, the week’s high).
▪️ Thursday: −$493B vs. +$581B (1.18x) on the day Huang resigned.
▪️ Friday (this afternoon): −$627B vs. +$376B (0.60x).

So through Thursday, the money leaving Nvidia was showing up, dollar for dollar or better, in its rivals. On the week through Thursday, AMD was up 30%, Broadcom 24% and Marvell 16%, while Nvidia was down 11%.

Friday is the first real crack. In a broad chip selloff (SOX -3.8%), the rivals are giving back far more than Nvidia, and their combined gain now covers only about 60% of Nvidia’s loss.

BofA adds a third hike to its Fed call, now calling for hikes at each of the next three meetings (December, January and March). That’s one more than Goldman, which added a March hike two days ago, and the same path as Deutsche Bank. Unlike Goldman, which sees the first cut in December 2027, BofA has no cuts penciled in for 2027 (or 2028 for that matter).

BofA’s Aditya Bhave (US Economic Weekly) says after October CPI the Fed “no longer has the luxury of hiking at a quarterly pace.” Instead of just pulling March forward, BofA added a hike because “the entire distribution of outcomes has now moved to the right.” BofA also noted Waller’s point that the Fed needs to take back at least last year’s 75 bp of “risk management” cuts. BofA thinks the Fed takes back one of its 2024 cuts too.

Risks both ways, per BofA:
▪️ Downside: “a reflexively dovish committee” could push the last hike to April or June, or skip it, on softer data, a US-Iran deal that pushes oil lower or a sharp equity selloff.
▪️ Upside: a tighter labor market and a jump in wage growth could take rates above 5%, as could another year of big start-of-year price increases.

They still look for 25 bp in December, not 50. BofA says “everything would have to break in favor of the hawks” for a half point, and lists five conditions:

▪️ October core PCE near 0.4% (BofA tracks 0.32%, out November 25).
▪️ November unemployment at 4.0% (October was 4.1%).
▪️ November wage growth of 0.4% (October already hit it).
▪️ More participants, particularly the doves, open to considering 50
▪️ Futures pricing at least a 50% chance of 50 bp (about 14% after CPI).

The debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes again to how many more times and how fast. Next up are the FOMC minutes Wednesday, which BofA expects to show a deeper split over the October pause than the 10-2 vote suggested.

Two more Fed officials signaled on Thursday they see more hikes ahead, but not of the 50 basis point variety. 

New York Fed President and FOMC vice chair John Williams and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly (2027 voter), traditionally in close alignment with the Fed’s old core of Powell, Jefferson and Williams, both spoke Thursday. As a reminder, Williams, an important voice, has been one of the more dovish members, tipping the October hold ahead of time and later noting that he thought a December hike would be the last under his base case.

▪️ Williams on direction: Inflation is “far too high” and stubbornly persistent, and the Fed still has work to do to get policy to the right place (via Bloomberg). That’s a step up from last week’s more subdued “appropriate time to accumulate more information.”

▪️ Williams on pace: The Fed will need to act “over time.” The economy is resilient and getting stronger but not overheating. He didn’t commit to a specific move in December.

▪️ Daly on direction: “My bias is that further tightening will be needed.” “We have a labor market that’s stable, growth that’s good, but we definitely have an inflation problem right now,” with price pressures spreading into services (via Reuters).

▪️ Daly on pace: Rising bond yields “are most welcome,” and tighter financial conditions give the Fed “a little more time to make really calibrated decisions.” On how much and when: “We have many more pieces of data and information over many, many quarters.”

That makes all 10 Fed officials who’ve spoken on the direction of rates since last Thursday’s selloff lean toward more hikes, but they’re split on how fast. I count four camps:

▪️ Quick, and possibly 50bp: Governor Waller, who said a 50bp hike “should be considered” if core CPI is “around 0.3% or even higher,” and that “hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk.”

▪️ Quicker pace, but not pushing for 50bp: Dallas’ Logan, who sees “at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases” and says “it may be possible to move more rapidly this winter,” and Cleveland’s Hammack, who wants “smaller increments, more frequent, smaller rises.”

▪️ Slower pace: New York’s Williams, the FOMC vice chair (act “over time”); San Francisco’s Daly (“a little more time to make really calibrated decisions”); Philadelphia’s Paulson (“further gradual tightening seems appropriate”); Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman (more tightening “has to be carefully weighed against its costs”); and Richmond’s Barkin (“it is wise to move policy with care”).

▪️ Worried about inflation, but don't want to prejudge decisions: Chicago’s Goolsbee (October CPI was “borderline disturbing”) and St. Louis’ Musalem (inflation is “a regressive tax”).

Among the six December voters who’ve weighed in, that’s one for quick and possibly 50bp, two for quicker quarter-point steps and three, including the FOMC vice chair, for a more measured pace. 

That makes 25bp in December the base case, with the real debate over how quickly the next hikes follow which will be teased out in the dot plot. October PCE and November payrolls, both out before the Dec. 8–9 meeting, will be key.

From @C_Barraud’s Thursday Morning Brief: While many think of Europe as the “anti-AI” trade, it was AI that got the credit for the UK’s strong GDP report Thursday morning.

UK GDP rose 0.7% in Q3, according to the ONS. That ties Q1 2024 for the fastest pace in two and a half years and is up from 0.5% in Q2, which was revised up from the 0.4% first estimate. The quarter matched the Bloomberg consensus, but September alone grew 0.2% versus a flat reading expected. August was revised down to flat from +0.1%.

The ONS said business-facing services drove the gain, with the rollout of AI fueling a 2.1% jump in information and communication output. The AI lift also showed up in factories:
▪️ Services output rose 0.9%, with professional, scientific and technical activities up 1.6%.
▪️ Manufacturing also rose 0.9%, led by a 4.6% surge in computer, electronic and optical products.
▪️ Business investment was 3% higher than a year earlier.
▪️ Consumer spending rose 0.6%, more than expected, and government spending was also up 0.6%.

Contributions were broad. Households and capital formation each added about a third of a point, while net trade was a small drag.

Among G7 economies, the UK has now grown the second-fastest through the first nine months of the year, behind just the US. France has contracted over the same stretch. Forecasters are scrambling to catch up. The BoE’s 2026 growth forecast is up about half a point since July, and the IMF and the Bloomberg survey median have each been revised up about 0.3 points.

So the UK isn’t really a hedge against the AI trade. At the margin, it’s levered to it. PwC’s Jake Finney warned that the growth remains concentrated in a small number of industries tied to the AI build-out. 

There’s also a rate angle. The BoE hiked last week for the first time in more than three years. After today’s data, markets still see a near 80% chance of another hike in December and three by next summer. The BoE expects inflation to approach 5% next year and growth to slow to 0.3% in Q4 and 0.2% per quarter through 2027. Energy bills are set to jump about a quarter in January when the price cap resets. Bloomberg Economics warns that if the strength carries into 2027, the BoE could end up taking rates above its 4.25% terminal projection.
